audit.pedagogicalValue: Balances rejected and preferred objects at the same structural level.

items.setupText: The reference letter should list three qualities as adjective phrases after 'is'.
items.taskText: Which version keeps that form for all three qualities?
options: He is reliable, patient, and works well with others.
He is reliable, patient, and good at solving problems.
He is reliable, has patience, and good at solving problems.
He has reliability, is patient, and good at solving problems.
items.answer: He is reliable, patient, and good at solving problems.
items.explanation: The single adjectives and the longer 'good at solving problems' phrase all serve as adjective descriptions after 'is'.

rationales.He is reliable, patient, and works well: The third member changes to a finite action instead of another adjective phrase after 'is'.
rationales.He is reliable, patient, and good at sol: The single adjectives and the longer 'good at solving problems' phrase all serve as adjective descriptions after 'is'.
rationales.He is reliable, has patience, and good a: 'Has patience' changes the second member into another verb phrase.
rationales.He has reliability, is patient, and good: The first member is a separate possession construction, not one of three adjective phrases sharing 'is'.

findings: Manual/team-review repeated the same infinitive choices and boilerplate messages.

audit.levelReason: Adult reference writing with accessible personal qualities.

items.setupText: The company changed from one activity to another. Both activity names follow prepositions.
items.taskText: Complete: 'We moved from selling furniture to ___ it.'
options: repair
repairing
repairs
repaired
items.answer: repairing
items.explanation: Selling furniture and repairing it are matching activity phrases after from and to.

rationales.repair: The 'to' in 'from ... to' is a preposition, so this verb naming the new activity takes '-ing'.
rationales.repairs: 'Repairs' is a finite verb form here, not an activity phrase after the preposition; as a noun it also cannot take 'it' as a direct object.
rationales.repairing: Selling furniture and repairing it are matching activity phrases after from and to.
rationales.repaired: A past participle does not name the new activity in this construction.

findings: Proposal/student-handbook repeated the original three-skill list without useful feedback.
audit.microSkill: From-ing to-ing transition between activities
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes prepositional 'to' in a transition rather than treating every to as infinitival.
audit.levelReason: A clear business change with two familiar activities.
audit.similarityNote: Transition endpoints, distinct from preference comparison with prefer-to.

items.setupText: Each explanation of the trip's purpose should begin with 'to' and an action verb.
items.taskText: Which version gives both purposes in that matching form?
options: We visited the depot to inspect the vans and a meeting with the drivers.
We visited the depot for an inspection and to meet the drivers.
We visited the depot to inspect the vans and we met the drivers.
We visited the depot to inspect the vans and to meet the drivers.
items.answer: We visited the depot to inspect the vans and to meet the drivers.
items.explanation: The two to-infinitives state parallel purposes of the same visit.

rationales.We visited the depot to inspect the vans: The second member names a meeting instead of giving an infinitival purpose.
rationales.We visited the depot for an inspection a: Both purposes may be understood, but the first uses a noun phrase after 'for' instead of the requested 'to' pattern.
rationales.We visited the depot to inspect the vans: This asserts a meeting as another event rather than presenting it in the requested purpose form.
The two to-infinitives state parallel purposes of the same visit.

findings: Receipt/policy-reminder improbably made a receipt teach skills and repeated all feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel purpose infinitives versus event assertions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes matching purposes from grammatically related but differently packaged information.
audit.levelReason: A practical work visit with two explicit aims.
audit.similarityNote: Purpose scope rather than the plans and obligations in earlier items.

items.setupText: The first action is ongoing, and the second is already complete. The writer must preserve those meanings, not force identical forms.
items.taskText: Which sentence correctly reports the two states of the booking work?
options: I'm checking the room list, and I've already sent the invitations.
I'm checking the room list, and I'm already sending the invitations.
I've checked the room list, and I've already sent the invitations.
I'm checking the room list, and I'll send the invitations later.
items.answer: I'm checking the room list, and I've already sent the invitations.
items.explanation: The two complete clauses are parallel in function while their verb forms preserve different stages of completion.

rationales.I'm checking the room list, and I've alr: The two complete clauses are parallel in function while their verb forms preserve different stages of completion.
rationales.I'm checking the room list, and I'm alre: This changes the completed sending into an ongoing action.
rationales.I've checked the room list, and I've alr: This changes the unfinished checking into a completed action.
rationales.I'm checking the room list, and I'll sen: This changes the completed sending into a future action.

findings: Agenda/support-call recycled the original infinitive list and generic judgments.
audit.microSkill: Parallel clauses retain necessary aspect differences
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids sacrificing accurate completion status for surface uniformity.
audit.levelReason: Common work updates distinguish progressive from present-perfect aspect.
audit.similarityNote: Same present reference time with different completion states, beyond A2's yesterday/now contrast.

items.setupText: One verb is 'wanted a refund'; the other is 'asked for a refund'. Keep both constructions complete.
items.taskText: Which sentence combines the two actions correctly?
options: She wanted and asked a refund.
She wanted for and asked for a refund.
She wanted a refund and asked one.
She wanted a refund and asked for one.
items.answer: She wanted a refund and asked for one.
items.explanation: Each verb keeps its required construction; 'one' avoids repeating 'a refund'.

'Asked' needs 'for' when the refund is the requested thing.
Each verb keeps its required construction; 'one' avoids repeating 'a refund'.
'Wanted' takes the refund directly and does not take 'for' in this meaning.
Without 'for', 'asked one' would need a different object such as a question, not the requested refund.

findings: Map/training-session repeated the same teaching list and did not address actual coordination demands.
audit.microSkill: Different coordinated verbs retain different complement requirements
audit.pedagogicalValue: Does not drop a required preposition merely to make coordinated verbs look alike.
audit.levelReason: A common service request with two familiar verb patterns.
audit.similarityNote: Correct difference in complement structure, not repetition of a common governing form.

items.setupText: An editor proposes changing 'hard' to 'hardly' in 'She worked quickly and hard' to match the -ly ending.
items.taskText: Which response preserves the intended meaning of fast, serious effort?
options: Keep 'quickly and hard'; different endings need not mean different grammatical roles.
Use 'quickly and hardly'; the ending makes both words describe manner.
Use 'quickly and easily'; easy work expresses the same effort as hard work.
Use 'quickly and briefly'; a short period of work expresses strong effort.
items.answer: Keep 'quickly and hard'; different endings need not mean different grammatical roles.
items.explanation: Quickly and hard both function as adverbs here. Their different endings preserve speed and effort without the near-negative meaning of hardly.

rationales.Use 'quickly and hardly'; the ending mak: 'Hardly' means almost not, not with effort. Matching endings would therefore change the meaning.
rationales.Use 'quickly and easily'; easy work expr: 'Easily' describes a lack of difficulty, not the serious effort expressed by 'hard'.
rationales.Keep 'quickly and hard'; different endin: Quickly and hard both function as adverbs here. Their different endings preserve speed and effort without the near-negative meaning of hardly.
rationales.Use 'quickly and briefly'; a short perio: 'Briefly' describes duration, not effort; someone may work briefly without working hard.

findings: Guide/before-filing original repeated the same three infinitives with no genuine variation.
audit.microSkill: Parallel adverbs need not share a suffix
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents a false parallelism repair that changes lexical meaning.
audit.levelReason: Familiar work description with a common hard/hardly confusion.
audit.similarityNote: Visible suffix mismatch is correct; form matching must respect meaning.

items.setupText: A says, 'I was tired, and I didn't stay for dessert.' B had the same experience.
items.taskText: Which short reply correctly matches both parts of A's statement?
options: So was I, and neither did I.
So did I, and neither was I.
Neither was I, and so did I.
So am I, and neither do I.
items.answer: So was I, and neither did I.
items.explanation: 'So was I' matches the positive be-clause, and 'neither did I' matches the negative past action.

The positive state needs 'was'; the negative past action needs 'did', so these auxiliaries are reversed.
This reverses the positive and negative meanings of the two experiences.
These present-tense auxiliaries do not match the past experiences being shared.
'So was I' matches the positive be-clause, and 'neither did I' matches the negative past action.

findings: Policy/project-checklist was another arbitrary frame variation with identical feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel agreement replies preserve auxiliary, tense and polarity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recovers the correct grammatical pattern from each of two antecedent clauses.
audit.levelReason: Common conversational agreement requires matching two familiar past constructions.
audit.similarityNote: Parallel response structure across speakers rather than editing a written list.

items.setupText: The timetable has two headings: 'Arrival time' and 'Leaving the station'. Both should name times, not activities.
items.taskText: Which replacement makes the second heading match the first in form and meaning?
options: Departure time
Departing passengers
Leave the station
The train has left
items.answer: Departure time
items.explanation: Both headings are noun phrases naming the time of a travel event.

rationales.Departure time: Both headings are noun phrases naming the time of a travel event.
rationales.Departing passengers: This names people rather than a time.
rationales.Leave the station: This is a command rather than a matching time heading.
rationales.The train has left: This is a completed-event statement, not a heading naming a time.

findings: Summary/tutor-explanation completed twenty near-duplicate infinitive lists with nonspecific feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel headings align both grammatical form and information type
audit.pedagogicalValue: Revises a mixed heading pair so readers can compare equivalent information.
audit.levelReason: Familiar timetable labels with a clear editing purpose.
audit.similarityNote: Information-label matching, distinct from commands or -ing task headings.

items.setupText: The event had plenty of interest but too little space. State the rejected and actual reasons for postponement in a balanced 'not ... but ...' contrast.
items.taskText: Which sentence accurately contrasts those reasons?
options: We postponed it not for lack of space but for lack of interest.
We postponed it not because interest was low but despite having enough space.
We postponed it not for lack of interest but for lack of space.
We postponed it not only for lack of interest but also for lack of space.
items.answer: We postponed it not for lack of interest but for lack of space.
items.explanation: The parallel for-phrases reject one causal explanation and supply the other, matching the stated circumstances.

rationales.We postponed it not for lack of space bu: This reverses the two reasons, rejecting the shortage of space and asserting insufficient interest.
rationales.We postponed it not for lack of interest: The parallel for-phrases reject one causal explanation and supply the other, matching the stated circumstances.
rationales.We postponed it not because interest was: The second phrase asserts enough space and expresses concession rather than the actual reason for postponement.
rationales.We postponed it not only for lack of int: 'Not only ... but also' adds both reasons; it does not reject lack of interest as required.

findings: The original request addressed students but repeated the elementary check/correct/send list and duplicated file in its audit-file tail.
audit.microSkill: Corrective causal pairing versus additive and concessive coordination
audit.pedagogicalValue: Use parallel reason phrases without reversing their polarity or adding a rejected cause.
audit.levelReason: B2 requires distinguishing corrective, additive and concessive relations in otherwise natural sentences.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike B1 refund alternatives, these are causal explanations and the foils change the logical relation.

items.setupText: The proposal offers two alternatives: reduce the booking fee or extend the opening hours. Put each whole verb phrase immediately after 'either' or 'or'.
items.taskText: Which version follows that alignment?
options: We can reduce either the booking fee or extend the opening hours.
Either we can reduce the booking fee or extend the opening hours.
We can reduce the booking fee either or extend the opening hours.
We can either reduce the booking fee or extend the opening hours.
items.answer: We can either reduce the booking fee or extend the opening hours.
items.explanation: Both markers introduce complete action phrases sharing 'We can'.

rationales.We can reduce either the booking fee or: The first marker introduces the noun 'the booking fee', while the second introduces an entire action.
rationales.Either we can reduce the booking fee or: This puts 'either' before the first clause rather than immediately before its verb phrase as requested.
rationales.We can either reduce the booking fee or: Both markers introduce complete action phrases sharing 'We can'.
rationales.We can reduce the booking fee either or: The first action has already ended before 'either', so the markers do not frame the alternatives.

findings: Teachers/policy-review original changed only the participant noun in twenty repeated infinitive lists.
audit.microSkill: Either-or placement around full verb-phrase alternatives
audit.pedagogicalValue: Aligns the markers with what is actually being contrasted.
audit.levelReason: Two extended policy actions require identifying phrase boundaries.
audit.similarityNote: Alternative action scope rather than B1's additive action pairing.

items.setupText: The comparison concerns the maintenance costs of two buildings, not the buildings themselves.
items.taskText: Complete: 'The library's maintenance costs exceed ___.'
options: the sports centre
maintaining the sports centre
those of the sports centre
the sports centre's facilities
items.answer: those of the sports centre
items.explanation: 'Those' stands for plural 'maintenance costs', keeping the comparison at the same level.

rationales.the sports centre: This makes a building the explicit comparison target instead of its costs.
rationales.maintaining the sports centre: This names an activity rather than the costs of that activity.
rationales.the sports centre's facilities: Facilities are features of the building, not the corresponding costs.
rationales.those of the sports centre: 'Those' stands for plural 'maintenance costs', keeping the comparison at the same level.

findings: Nurses/budget-meeting repeated the same three requested actions with generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Plural nominal substitution in a like-for-like comparison
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recovers the plural comparison noun with 'those of'.
audit.levelReason: An institutional cost comparison uses a compressed but precise second term.
audit.similarityNote: Plural demonstrative substitution rather than the B1 possessive ellipsis.

items.setupText: Both questions are reported indirectly after 'asked'.
items.taskText: Which version gives the two questions in consistent embedded form?
options: She asked where was the van parked and who had the keys.
She asked where the van was parked and who did have the keys?
She asked where the van was parked and where were the keys.
She asked where the van was parked and who had the keys.
items.answer: She asked where the van was parked and who had the keys.
items.explanation: Both clauses are embedded questions. The first uses statement order; the second naturally has subject 'who' before 'had'.

rationales.She asked where the van was parked and w: Both clauses are embedded questions. The first uses statement order; the second naturally has subject 'who' before 'had'.
rationales.She asked where was the van parked and w: The first clause incorrectly uses direct-question inversion after 'asked'.
rationales.She asked where the van was parked and w: The added direct-question marking does not match the requested indirect report of both questions.
The second question switches to direct-question inversion, and it changes the question from the key-holder to the keys' location.

findings: Clerks/manager-briefing original repeated a low-level list and awkwardly repeated manager.
audit.microSkill: Coordinated subject and nonsubject embedded questions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Matches embedded function without forcing identical visible word order on different wh-roles.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing subject who from a locative wh-question.
audit.similarityNote: Indirect-question coordination, not two that-statements or repeated relatives.

items.setupText: An editor objects to 'I understand your concern and why you raised it' because one complement is a noun phrase and the other a clause.
items.taskText: Which assessment correctly identifies what the coordination expresses?
options: The second member gives the speaker's reason for understanding the concern.
The second member reports why the listener understands the speaker's concern.
Both members identify what the speaker understands, despite their different forms.
The first member expresses understanding, but the second asks the listener for a reason.
items.answer: Both members identify what the speaker understands, despite their different forms.
items.explanation: Both complements belong to understand: the concern itself and the reason it was raised. Shared function permits these different forms.

rationales.The second member gives the speaker's re: Why you raised it is itself something understood, not a because-clause explaining the speaker's understanding.
rationales.Both members identify what the speaker u: Both complements belong to understand: the concern itself and the reason it was raised. Shared function permits these different forms.
rationales.The second member reports why the listen: The subject of 'understand' remains 'I'; 'you' is the subject only of 'raised' in the embedded clause.
rationales.The first member expresses understanding: The embedded why-clause is not a direct request for information; the speaker says that reason is understood.

findings: Drivers/complaint-review original offered the same form choices and boilerplate messages.
audit.microSkill: Coordination of unlike forms with a shared complement function
audit.pedagogicalValue: Rejects an overstrict surface-form rule when the verb licenses both complements.
audit.levelReason: Requires considering a noun phrase and an embedded question as equivalent arguments.
audit.similarityNote: Mixed object forms, beyond A2's mixed predicative descriptions.

items.setupText: The panel selected Hana for interview; Hana then accepted the invitation. Keep both facts and make Hana the subject of both coordinated parts.
items.taskText: Which version preserves her different roles in the two events?
options: Hana was selected for interview and accepted the invitation.
Hana selected the panel for interview and accepted the invitation.
Hana was selected for interview and was accepted the invitation.
Hana selected the invitation and was accepted for interview.
items.answer: Hana was selected for interview and accepted the invitation.
items.explanation: The first predicate is passive and the second active, correctly reflecting what was done to Hana and what she did.

rationales.Hana selected the panel for interview an: This makes Hana the person selecting the panel, reversing the first event's roles.
rationales.Hana was selected for interview and was: 'Accepted the invitation' is active; the extra 'was' does not form a grammatical passive with that object.
rationales.Hana was selected for interview and acce: The first predicate is passive and the second active, correctly reflecting what was done to Hana and what she did.
rationales.Hana selected the invitation and was acc: This changes both actions and their objects rather than preserving selection by the panel and acceptance by Hana.

findings: Volunteers/data-check repeated checking data both in the action and tail, with generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Intentional voice difference preserves coordinated subject roles
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids forcing both coordinated predicates into the same voice when that would change agency.
audit.levelReason: Requires comparing active and passive role assignments in a two-event account.
audit.similarityNote: Voice difference is necessary for meaning, unlike the B1 active-style CV task.

items.setupText: A repair took three days. Replacing the device had been expected to take one day, but replacement was not attempted.
items.taskText: Which comparison preserves the distinction between an actual duration and an estimate?
options: The repair took longer than replacement was expected to take.
The repair took longer than the replacement took.
The repair was expected to take longer than replacement was expected to take.
The repair started later than replacement was expected to start.
items.answer: The repair took longer than replacement was expected to take.
items.explanation: The comparative clauses share the duration meaning of take but retain their different evidence: measured repair time and expected replacement time.

rationales.The repair took longer than the replacem: This treats the replacement duration as an observed event, although no replacement occurred.
rationales.The repair was expected to take longer t: This changes the observed repair duration into an estimate as well, losing the actual-versus-estimated distinction.
rationales.The repair started later than replacemen: Starting later concerns the start time, not the duration of the two processes.
rationales.The repair took longer than replacement: The comparative clauses share the duration meaning of take but retain their different evidence: measured repair time and expected replacement time.

findings: The researchers original repeated check/correct/send with no B2-level comparison or diagnostic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel duration comparison with actual and estimated events
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keep comparison terms aligned without presenting an unperformed alternative as observed.
audit.levelReason: B2 combines a comparative clause with the distinction between a measured event and a projected alternative.
audit.similarityNote: Different from simpler price comparisons: the processes are comparable, but their evidential status must differ.

items.setupText: Compare 'We cannot fund both the archive and the exhibition' with 'We can fund neither the archive nor the exhibition.'
items.taskText: Which distinction between the paired alternatives is accurate?
options: The first rules out funding the pair together; the second rules out each project.
Both sentences say that neither project can receive any funding.
The first promises funding for exactly one project; the second postpones the choice.
The first gives priority to the archive; the second gives priority to the exhibition.
items.answer: The first rules out funding the pair together; the second rules out each project.
items.explanation: Negating 'both' rejects the combination without deciding each case; 'neither ... nor ...' excludes both individually.

rationales.The first rules out funding the pair tog: Negating 'both' rejects the combination without deciding each case; 'neither ... nor ...' excludes both individually.
rationales.Both sentences say that neither project: 'Not both' leaves open the possibility of funding one, unlike 'neither'.
rationales.The first promises funding for exactly o: The first does not guarantee that one will be funded, and the second excludes rather than postpones both.
rationales.The first gives priority to the archive;: The order of the paired nouns does not establish either priority.

findings: Visitors/contract-signing used an arbitrary time clause around a repeated elementary infinitive list.
audit.microSkill: Not-both versus neither-nor scope over a parallel pair
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes rejection of a combination from exclusion of each member.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting negation scope within familiar funding alternatives.
audit.similarityNote: Logical scope of a correlative pair, not basic connector selection.

items.setupText: The equipment note should list two passive requirements, each beginning with 'to be', as complements of 'needs'.
items.taskText: Which version follows that explicit pattern?
options: The scanner needs to be cleaned and to be recalibrated.
The scanner needs to be cleaned and recalibrating.
The scanner needs cleaning and to be recalibrated.
The scanner needs to be cleaned and the technician must recalibrate it.
items.answer: The scanner needs to be cleaned and to be recalibrated.
items.explanation: Both requirements use passive to-infinitives governed by 'needs'.

rationales.The scanner needs to be cleaned and reca: The second member switches to -ing rather than repeating the requested passive infinitive.
rationales.The scanner needs to be cleaned and to b: Both requirements use passive to-infinitives governed by 'needs'.
rationales.The scanner needs cleaning and to be rec: 'Needs cleaning' is grammatical, but it does not follow the specified repeated 'to be' style.
rationales.The scanner needs to be cleaned and the: The second clause is a grammatical instruction to a technician, not another passive complement of 'needs'.

findings: Managers/customer-update duplicated manager in the original and repeated all three actions and feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel passive infinitival complements under a stated style
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a chosen uniform construction from other legitimate expressions of need.
audit.levelReason: Technical maintenance requirements include passive infinitive and -ing alternatives.
audit.similarityNote: Passive complements of need; valid needs-cleaning is explicitly acknowledged.

items.setupText: The handbook should promise instructions for two procedures, not a procedure plus a reason or fact.
items.taskText: Which version keeps the promised content parallel in purpose?
options: It explains how to upload a photo and how to resize it.
It explains how to upload a photo and why the file size matters.
It explains how to upload a photo and that large files take longer.
It explains how to upload a photo and whether the image is suitable.
items.answer: It explains how to upload a photo and how to resize it.
items.explanation: Both how-to clauses promise procedures the reader can follow.

rationales.It explains how to upload a photo and wh: This pairs a procedure with an explanation of significance, not another procedure.
rationales.It explains how to upload a photo and th: This pairs a procedure with a fact about large files.
rationales.It explains how to upload a photo and ho: Both how-to clauses promise procedures the reader can follow.
rationales.It explains how to upload a photo and wh: This pairs a procedure with an assessment question about suitability.

findings: Applicants/planning-call repeated the same checking/correcting/sending list and generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel information functions in coordinated wh-complements
audit.pedagogicalValue: Matches what readers will learn, not merely the presence of a wh-word.
audit.levelReason: Four grammatical complements require distinguishing procedure, reason, fact and assessment.
audit.similarityNote: Semantic parallelism among well-formed clauses rather than an elementary form correction.

items.setupText: The team debated a new rota and then reached agreement on that rota. Record both completed events in one sentence.
items.taskText: Which concise coordination retains both events and their shared topic?
options: The team discussed whether to agree on a new rota.
The team agreed to discuss a new rota.
The team discussed changing the rota it had agreed on.
The team discussed and agreed on a new rota.
items.answer: The team discussed and agreed on a new rota.
items.explanation: The final noun phrase supplies the topic of 'discussed' and the object of 'on' after 'agreed'. Both completed actions are asserted.

rationales.The team discussed whether to agree on a: This reports discussion of a possible agreement, not that agreement was reached.
rationales.The team discussed and agreed on a new r: The final noun phrase supplies the topic of 'discussed' and the object of 'on' after 'agreed'. Both completed actions are asserted.
This reports an agreement to have a discussion, not a completed discussion followed by agreement on its content.
rationales.The team discussed changing the rota it: This introduces a discussion about changing an earlier agreement, rather than the stated process of reaching the new one.

findings: Workers/hiring-process original repeated the same manager request and generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Shared object with a direct-object verb and a prepositional verb
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves different complement patterns within compact coordination.
audit.levelReason: Requires recovering a final object as part of two differently built predicates.
audit.similarityNote: Shared final object, extending B1's fully restated wanted/asked-for constructions.

items.setupText: The intended meaning compares two people's trust in Leo: Mara trusts him more than the speaker does.
items.taskText: Which comparison makes those two subjects explicit?
options: Mara trusts Leo more than me.
Mara trusts Leo more than she trusts me.
Mara trusts Leo more than I do.
Mara trusts me more than Leo does.
items.answer: Mara trusts Leo more than I do.
items.explanation: 'I do' recovers 'I trust Leo', so the comparison clearly pairs Mara's trust with the speaker's.

This can be read as comparing Leo and the speaker as objects of Mara's trust; it does not make the intended subjects explicit.
This explicitly compares the two objects of Mara's trust, not two people's trust in Leo.
'I do' recovers 'I trust Leo', so the comparison clearly pairs Mara's trust with the speaker's.
This compares Mara's and Leo's trust in the speaker, changing both the comparison subjects and its object.

findings: Parents/project-dashboard original changed only the participant and tail of an elementary request list.
audit.microSkill: Explicit comparative clause resolves subject-object ambiguity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses a recoverable predicate to show which grammatical roles are being compared.
audit.levelReason: Requires tracking two possible comparisons without rejecting informal object-case variants as universally wrong.
audit.similarityNote: People as competing subjects or objects, not noun-class comparison such as costs.

items.setupText: The writer wants both adjectives to keep their usual prepositions: 'interested in' and 'committed to'.
items.taskText: Which sentence achieves that while sharing the activity phrase?
options: She is interested and committed to improving the service.
She is interested in and committed in improving the service.
She is interested to and committed to improving the service.
She is interested in and committed to improving the service.
items.answer: She is interested in and committed to improving the service.
items.explanation: The two adjectives retain their different prepositions and share 'improving the service'.

rationales.She is interested and committed to impro: The shared 'to' does not supply the required 'in' after 'interested' in this activity meaning.
rationales.She is interested to and committed to im: 'Interested' takes 'in' when referring to involvement in an activity here.
rationales.She is interested in and committed to im: The two adjectives retain their different prepositions and share 'improving the service'.

findings: Assistants/board-discussion repeated all three infinitives and boilerplate messages.
audit.microSkill: Shared activity complement after differently governed adjectives
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps required prepositions rather than forcing superficial sameness.
audit.levelReason: Two extended adjective complements require recognition of different lexical patterns.
audit.similarityNote: Adjective government rather than coordinated verbs sharing an object.

items.setupText: Begin with 'Not only' and pair two complete claims about the library's improvement. Use standard formal word order.
items.taskText: Which version correctly forms the initial clause?
options: Not only the library did extend its hours, but it also added a delivery service.
Not only extended the library its hours, but it also added a delivery service.
Not only the library extended its hours, but it also added a delivery service.
Not only did the library extend its hours, but it also added a delivery service.
items.answer: Not only did the library extend its hours, but it also added a delivery service.

rationales.Not only did the library extend its hour: Initial 'Not only' gives the first clause auxiliary-subject order: 'did the library extend'.
rationales.Not only the library did extend its hour: The auxiliary must precede the subject in this fronted negative-additive construction.
rationales.Not only extended the library its hours,: The simple-past clause needs auxiliary 'did' for inversion; moving only the main verb does not work.
rationales.Not only the library extended its hours,: The initial 'Not only' clause requires inversion in the stated formal construction.

findings: Tutors/revised-procedure original was the same basic infinitive list with an appended context.

items.setupText: The consultant accepted the inspection task but refused the authorisation task. Keep that difference within a balanced pair of infinitives.

items.answer: She agreed to inspect the building but not to authorise its use.
items.explanation: The two infinitives share 'agreed', with 'not' applied only to the authorisation task.

rationales.She agreed not to inspect the building b: This reverses the accepted and refused tasks.
rationales.She agreed to inspect the building but n: The two infinitives share 'agreed', with 'not' applied only to the authorisation task.
rationales.She agreed to inspect and to authorise t: This accepts both actions and removes the stated refusal.

findings: Trainees/service-report original repeated checking/correcting/sending with no meaningful B2 distinction.
audit.microSkill: Positive-negative parallel infinitives with local negation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps two comparable tasks balanced without making their polarity identical.
audit.levelReason: Requires tracking agreement and refusal within a coordinated complement.

items.setupText: The report should name three measured qualities as nouns, not two qualities followed by an activity.

items.answer: We measured cost, reliability, and customer satisfaction.

rationales.We measured cost, reliability, and custo: The final member becomes a separate assertion about customers instead of another measured quality.
All three noun phrases name qualities being measured, including the level of customer satisfaction.

items.setupText: The instructions tell two separate groups to do different things: applicants must sign the form, while referees must attach a letter.
items.taskText: Which parallel pair of instructions keeps each action with the right group?

Applicants must sign the form, and referees must attach a letter.
Applicants and referees must sign the form and attach a letter.
Referees must ask applicants to sign the form and attach a letter.
items.answer: Applicants must sign the form, and referees must attach a letter.
items.explanation: Repeating a full subject-and-duty clause keeps each obligation with its own group; sharing the subject would blur that distribution.

rationales.Applicants must sign the form and attach: Both actions now belong to applicants; the letter's source does not make referees responsible for attaching it.
rationales.Applicants and referees must sign the fo: The shared subject groups applicants and referees under the whole pair of duties instead of making their separate duties explicit.
rationales.Referees must ask applicants to sign the: Both infinitives can belong to what referees ask applicants to do; this does not explicitly assign attachment to referees.
rationales.Applicants must sign the form, and refer: Repeating a full subject-and-duty clause keeps each obligation with its own group; sharing the subject would blur that distribution.

audit.levelReason: B2 requires resolving task allocation through clause-level versus phrase-level coordination.
audit.similarityNote: Replaces the duplicate procedural-content contrast; here the two actions have different required actors.

items.setupText: The intended comparison is between what the landlord promised and what the landlord actually provided.
items.taskText: Which version makes those two objects parallel and explicit?
options: There is a gap between the landlord and what was provided.
There is a gap between what the landlord promised and what the landlord provided.
There is a gap between promising the landlord and what was provided.
There is a gap between what the landlord promised and who provided it.
items.answer: There is a gap between what the landlord promised and what the landlord provided.
items.explanation: The two what-clauses name the promised and actual provisions as matching objects of comparison.

rationales.There is a gap between what the landlord: The two what-clauses name the promised and actual provisions as matching objects of comparison.
rationales.There is a gap between the landlord and: This compares a person with what was provided, not the promised and actual provisions.
rationales.There is a gap between promising the lan: This changes the landlord from the person making the promise to its recipient.
rationales.There is a gap between what the landlord: This compares promised content with the identity of a provider, not actual provision.

findings: Coordinators/compliance-check repeated the same request frame and undiagnostic messages.
audit.microSkill: Parallel what-clauses as comparison objects
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps both the semantic category and agent role stable in a comparison.
audit.levelReason: Two clausal noun-like complements require tracking roles and reference.
audit.similarityNote: Promised-versus-provided content, not how-to procedures.

items.setupText: Repairs are complete; inspection is happening now. Keep both actions passive and preserve their different stages.
items.taskText: Which sentence accurately balances the two status reports?
options: The bridge is being repaired and inspected.
The bridge has been repaired and is now being inspected.
The bridge has been repaired and inspected.
The bridge will be repaired and is now being inspected.
items.answer: The bridge has been repaired and is now being inspected.
items.explanation: The distinct auxiliary phrases keep repair completed and inspection in progress while both predicates remain passive.

rationales.The bridge is being repaired and inspect: This presents repair as ongoing as well as inspection, instead of completed.
rationales.The bridge has been repaired and is now: The distinct auxiliary phrases keep repair completed and inspection in progress while both predicates remain passive.
rationales.The bridge has been repaired and inspect: This presents inspection as completed along with repair.
rationales.The bridge will be repaired and is now b: This moves repair into the future, contrary to the completed repair status.

findings: Guests/evaluation-memo used an implausible participant setting and repeated the same infinitive demand.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Retains separate auxiliaries when sharing one would change completion meaning.
audit.levelReason: Requires combining passive voice with perfect and progressive aspect.
audit.similarityNote: Auxiliary recovery in two passives, beyond the B1 active status contrast.

items.setupText: The assessment compares whether a rule is clear with whether the same rule is useful. State both criteria as matching whether-clauses.
items.taskText: Which version preserves the two criteria in that form?
options: We considered whether the rule was clear and useful guidance.
We considered whether the rule was clear and making it useful.
We considered whether the rule was clear and whether it was useful.
We considered whether the rule was clear and its usefulness.
items.answer: We considered whether the rule was clear and whether it was useful.
items.explanation: Both clauses express evaluation questions about the same rule, with 'it' retaining the reference.

rationales.We considered whether the rule was clear: The second member becomes a noun phrase, not a matching whether-clause about the rule.
This changes the second criterion into an activity of improving the rule.
Both clauses express evaluation questions about the same rule, with 'it' retaining the reference.
The noun phrase is grammatical as a complement of 'considered', but it does not meet the specified repeated whether-clause style.

findings: Interns/final-interview completed twenty repeated manager requests with generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Parallel whether-clauses with stable referential focus
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps evaluation questions at the same structural level while allowing pronoun reference.
audit.levelReason: An explicit editorial style distinguishes a clause pair from other grammatical complement types.
audit.similarityNote: Evaluative alternatives rather than procedural how-to clauses or asserted that-content.

items.setupText: The critic writes: 'The renovation was not so much a restoration as a reinvention.'
items.taskText: How does the balanced pair characterize the renovation?
options: It gives restoration and reinvention equal weight as independent achievements.
It presents reinvention as the more accurate description.
It says the renovation failed to qualify as either restoration or reinvention.
It makes successful restoration a prerequisite for later reinvention.
items.answer: It presents reinvention as the more accurate description.
items.explanation: The parallel noun phrases offer competing labels, with the second preferred as a characterization.

rationales.It gives restoration and reinvention equ: 'Not so much ... as ...' shifts emphasis from the first description to the second, rather than balancing their importance equally.
rationales.It presents reinvention as the more accu: The parallel noun phrases offer competing labels, with the second preferred as a characterization.
rationales.It says the renovation failed to qualify: The second label is endorsed, not rejected with the first.
rationales.It makes successful restoration a prereq: The construction contrasts descriptions; it does not establish a necessary sequence of stages.

findings: Report/committee-review original tested elementary infinitive matching under a C1 label.
audit.microSkill: Not-so-much/as recharacterization with parallel noun phrases
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes rhetorical reclassification from addition, exclusion or temporal sequence.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting the relationship between two plausible evaluative labels.
audit.similarityNote: Degree of descriptive fit, not the simple not-but correction at B1.

items.setupText: Compare 'Both reviewers challenged the method and the conclusion' with 'The reviewers challenged both the method and the conclusion.'
items.taskText: Which distinction is made explicit by moving 'both'?
options: The first presents two challenges; the second says there were exactly two reviewers.
The first excludes disagreement between the reviewers; the second establishes such disagreement.
The first says each reviewer challenged only one aspect; the second assigns one aspect to each reviewer.
The first explicitly counts the reviewers as two; the second explicitly includes two challenged aspects.
items.answer: The first explicitly counts the reviewers as two; the second explicitly includes two challenged aspects.
items.explanation: Before 'reviewers', 'both' quantifies the subject; before 'the method', it coordinates the challenged objects.

rationales.The first presents two challenges; the s: This reverses what the marker explicitly pairs in the two sentences.
rationales.The first excludes disagreement between: Neither placement states whether the reviewers agreed with each other on every point.
rationales.The first explicitly counts the reviewer: Before 'reviewers', 'both' quantifies the subject; before 'the method', it coordinates the challenged objects.
rationales.The first says each reviewer challenged: The marker does not distribute one aspect to each reviewer; that pairing is not stated.

findings: Schedule/methodology-section original repeated the same to-reduce/improve/protect frame and boilerplate.
audit.microSkill: Correlative scope changes between subject and object positions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Reads marker placement as a difference in explicit grouping, not just surface balance.
audit.levelReason: Requires comparing grammatical scope while avoiding unsupported distributive inferences.
audit.similarityNote: Subject quantification versus object inclusion, beyond B1 placement exercises.

items.setupText: The museum's statement should keep both propositions under 'believes', without independently asserting either as established fact.
items.taskText: Which version makes that parallel attribution unambiguous?
options: The museum believes that the portrait is genuine, and the signature is original.
The museum believes the portrait is genuine and takes the signature as proof of its origin.
The museum believes both that the portrait is genuine and that the signature is original.
The museum believes the portrait is genuine because the signature is original.
items.answer: The museum believes both that the portrait is genuine and that the signature is original.
items.explanation: The paired that-clauses are both complements of believes, keeping the attribution explicit for each proposition.

rationales.The museum believes that the portrait is: The second coordinated clause can be read as the writer's separate assertion; it lacks explicit inclusion under believes.
rationales.The museum believes the portrait is genu: This turns the second claim into the museum's use of the signature as proof, rather than explicitly reporting a belief in the signature's originality.
This gives the signature's originality as a reason for the first belief instead of presenting two separately attributed beliefs.
rationales.The museum believes both that the portra: The paired that-clauses are both complements of believes, keeping the attribution explicit for each proposition.

findings: Form/stakeholder-meeting original gave only basic form matching with an appended academic setting.
audit.microSkill: Both-that/and-that makes shared belief attribution explicit
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses balanced embedding to avoid promoting an attributed proposition into an independent fact.
audit.levelReason: Requires scope-sensitive comparison of several otherwise interpretable reports.
audit.similarityNote: Coordination under a belief predicate, not a sentence-boundary editing task.

items.setupText: Site A's figure is complaints per thousand completed orders. The report must compare the same measure at Site B.
items.taskText: Which second term gives a genuinely parallel comparison?
options: Site A's complaint rate exceeds the number of complaints received by Site B.
Site A's complaint rate exceeds Site B's rate per thousand enquiries.
Site A's complaint rate exceeds the proportion of Site B's staff handling complaints.
Site A's complaint rate exceeds Site B's rate per thousand completed orders.
items.answer: Site A's complaint rate exceeds Site B's rate per thousand completed orders.
items.explanation: Both terms use complaints relative to the same denominator: completed orders.

rationales.Site A's complaint rate exceeds Site B's: Both terms use complaints relative to the same denominator: completed orders.
rationales.Site A's complaint rate exceeds the numb: A rate is being compared with a raw count rather than the same measure.
rationales.Site A's complaint rate exceeds Site B's: The denominator changes from completed orders to enquiries, so the measures are not equivalent.
rationales.Site A's complaint rate exceeds the prop: This compares complaint frequency with a staffing proportion, despite similar numerical wording.

findings: Notice/recommendation original used the same infinitive list and generic feedback despite its advanced band.
audit.microSkill: Semantic parallelism of comparison measures and denominators
audit.pedagogicalValue: Checks that grammatically balanced numerical expressions measure the same thing.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing rates, counts and different comparison bases without arithmetic.
audit.similarityNote: Metric comparability, not the simpler person-versus-salary mismatch.

items.setupText: 'Obtaining permission is harder for small firms than renewing it is for large ones.' An editor wants to expand this comparison without changing either the processes or the groups compared.
items.taskText: Which expansion preserves both dimensions of the comparison?
options: Small firms find obtaining permission harder than large firms find obtaining it.
Small firms find obtaining permission harder than they find renewing it.
Small firms find obtaining permission harder than large firms find renewing it.
Small firms find renewing permission harder than large firms find obtaining it.
items.answer: Small firms find obtaining permission harder than large firms find renewing it.
items.explanation: The first side concerns small firms obtaining permission; the second concerns large firms renewing it. Both differences survive the expansion.

rationales.Small firms find obtaining permission ha: This keeps the group contrast but compares obtaining on both sides, removing the original contrast between obtaining and renewing.
The first side concerns small firms obtaining permission; the second concerns large firms renewing it. Both differences survive the expansion.
This keeps the process contrast but makes small firms the group on both sides.
rationales.Small firms find renewing permission har: Both dimensions still vary, but the processes assigned to the two groups are reversed.

findings: The email design-to-reduce original repeated elementary infinitive forms despite the evidence-comparison tail.
audit.microSkill: Two-dimensional alignment in an expanded comparative
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserve both a process contrast and a group contrast instead of standardizing away one of them.
audit.levelReason: C1 requires tracking paired processes and beneficiaries across an elliptical comparison.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike lower-level like-with-like comparisons, the intended comparison deliberately varies two dimensions.

items.setupText: The production note reads: 'Tomas supervised the lighting, and Leila the sound.'
items.taskText: Which expansion preserves the parallel relationship licensed by the omitted verb?
options: Tomas supervised Leila, who was responsible for the sound and lighting.
Tomas and Leila jointly supervised both lighting and sound.
Tomas supervised the lighting, and Leila supervised the sound.
Tomas supervised the lighting, and the sound was supervised by his team.
items.answer: Tomas supervised the lighting, and Leila supervised the sound.
items.explanation: The second clause omits the recoverable 'supervised', with its subject and object aligned against those of the first.

rationales.Tomas supervised Leila, who was responsi: The original makes Leila a parallel subject, not an object of Tomas's supervision.
rationales.Tomas and Leila jointly supervised both: The structure assigns contrasting areas to the two people; it does not say both responsibilities were shared.
rationales.Tomas supervised the lighting, and Leila: The second clause omits the recoverable 'supervised', with its subject and object aligned against those of the first.
rationales.Tomas supervised the lighting, and the s: This replaces Leila with Tomas's team as the supervisor of sound.

findings: Chart/compliance-review original changed nouns and tails around the same simple infinitive list.
audit.microSkill: Subject-object alignment in verbal gapping
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recovers omitted wording without changing the allocation of roles.
audit.levelReason: Requires interpreting two contrasted remnants in an elliptical clause.
audit.similarityNote: Role mapping in gapping, not merely recognizing a semicolon or fragment.

items.setupText: A novelist writes: 'By midnight, he had lost his ticket and his patience.'
items.taskText: Which editorial assessment best accounts for the coordinated objects?
options: The verb keeps its physical-misplacement meaning for both objects.
The coordination explicitly makes the missing ticket the cause of his impatience.
The whole phrase means frustration, without reporting an actual missing ticket.
One verb links a literal loss with a figurative one.
items.answer: One verb links a literal loss with a figurative one.
items.explanation: Lose combines naturally with the physical ticket and, figuratively, with patience. Their coordination creates the literary effect without requiring identical senses.

rationales.The verb keeps its physical-misplacement: 'Losing patience' is a change of emotional state, not physical misplacement. Sharing the verb does not force the same lexical sense.
rationales.The coordination explicitly makes the mi: The missing ticket may explain his impatience in a fuller story, but and does not explicitly state that causal link.
rationales.The whole phrase means frustration, with: The familiar figurative sense of losing patience does not cancel the literal report that the ticket was lost.
rationales.One verb links a literal loss with a fig: Lose combines naturally with the physical ticket and, figuratively, with patience. Their coordination creates the literary effect without requiring identical senses.

findings: Application/evaluation-form original tested an elementary list despite the C1 label.
audit.microSkill: Deliberate literal-figurative coordination
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes rhetorical play from a failed attempt at grammatical parallelism.
audit.levelReason: Requires sensitivity to genre and two licensed senses of a shared verb.
audit.similarityNote: A semantic asymmetry is purposeful rather than a comparison error.

items.setupText: In 'The director asked the producer to revise the budget and approved the new schedule', who performs the two relevant actions?
items.taskText: Which reading follows the coordination of the finite verbs?
options: The producer is asked both to revise the budget and to approve the schedule.
The producer is asked to revise the budget; the director approves the schedule.
The director revises the budget and asks the producer to approve the schedule.
The director asks for both actions but does not perform either one.
items.answer: The producer is asked to revise the budget; the director approves the schedule.
items.explanation: 'Asked' and 'approved' are parallel finite verbs with subject 'The director'; 'to revise' belongs inside the first verb's complement.

rationales.The producer is asked to revise the budg: 'Asked' and 'approved' are parallel finite verbs with subject 'The director'; 'to revise' belongs inside the first verb's complement.
rationales.The producer is asked both to revise the: That meaning would require 'to revise ... and approve ...', without the finite past form 'approved'.
rationales.The director revises the budget and asks: The director asks the producer to revise; the text does not say the director performs that revision.
rationales.The director asks for both actions but d: The finite 'approved' asserts an action by the director rather than a second request.

findings: Message/pilot-program original repeated the same low-level infinitive choices and generic messages.
audit.microSkill: Distinguishing outer finite coordination from inner infinitive coordination
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses parallel verb form to identify the correct actor across an embedded complement.
audit.levelReason: Requires parsing two possible coordination levels and their agent roles.
audit.similarityNote: Nested agency, not simple shared-subject verb agreement.

items.setupText: The writer wants to retain two grounds for concern as objects of 'about': the delays and whether the budget is sufficient.
items.taskText: Which judgment is appropriate for 'We are concerned about the delays and whether the budget is sufficient'?
options: It is acceptable: the noun phrase and question clause share the concern-complement role.
It is faulty because 'about' can introduce only noun phrases, not a whether-clause.
It means the delays determine whether the budget is sufficient, rather than naming two concerns.
It places only the delays under 'concerned', while asserting budget sufficiency as a fact.
items.answer: It is acceptable: the noun phrase and question clause share the concern-complement role.
items.explanation: The two forms can be coordinated because both name what the concern is about.

rationales.It is faulty because 'about' can introdu: 'About whether...' is a legitimate prepositional complement; a noun phrase is not the only possible form.
rationales.It is acceptable: the noun phrase and qu: The two forms can be coordinated because both name what the concern is about.
rationales.It means the delays determine whether th: The coordination adds concerns; it does not assert that one determines the answer to the other.
rationales.It places only the delays under 'concern: The whether-clause remains an unresolved issue within the concern, not an assertion of sufficiency.

findings: Contract/findings-published original was a repeated designed-to list without advanced decisions.
audit.microSkill: Mixed nominal and interrogative complements of a shared preposition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes functional parallelism without requiring identical complement categories.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing a question under a preposition from an independently asserted clause.
audit.similarityNote: Preposition-governed coordination, extending but not repeating the B2 understand example's verb government.

items.setupText: The note must preserve a past investigation and a current unresolved question: the team established how the leak began, but it still does not know how to prevent another one.
items.taskText: Which sentence retains that contrast without imposing false formal symmetry?
options: The team established how the leak began and how another one was prevented.
The team established how the leak began but not how to prevent another one.
The team established how to begin the leak but not how to prevent another one.
The team established that the leak began but not that another one was prevented.
items.answer: The team established how the leak began but not how to prevent another one.
items.explanation: Both how-clauses are complements of 'established', but their different forms correctly distinguish a past event from a prospective procedure.

rationales.The team established how the leak began: This changes the unresolved prevention procedure into a completed event that the team established.
rationales.The team established how to begin the le: This turns the investigation of a cause into instructions for causing a leak.
rationales.The team established how the leak began: Both how-clauses are complements of 'established', but their different forms correctly distinguish a past event from a prospective procedure.
rationales.The team established that the leak began: This substitutes facts about occurrence and prevention for the original questions about cause and method.

findings: Invoice/grant-application original used the same elementary form contrast under academic wording.
audit.microSkill: Finite and infinitival question complements preserve distinct temporal functions
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids rewriting a legitimate coordination merely to make the embedded forms identical.
audit.levelReason: Requires maintaining past causal knowledge and unresolved future procedure within a contrasted pair.
audit.similarityNote: Necessary differences inside parallel interrogative complements, not a uniform how-to style exercise.

items.setupText: Repair 'The firm has, and will continue to, support local clubs.' Retain the firm's past support for clubs and its commitment to continue that same support.
items.taskText: Which revision repairs the shared verb while preserving both relationships?
options: The firm has local support and will continue to support clubs.
The firm has been supported by local clubs and will continue to support them.
The firm has supported local clubs and will continue to support them.
The firm has supported local clubs and hopes they will continue to support it.
items.answer: The firm has supported local clubs and will continue to support them.
items.explanation: 'Has' needs 'supported', whereas 'continue to' needs 'support'. Giving each construction its required form preserves the firm as provider in both claims.

rationales.The firm has local support and will cont: Has local support makes the firm a recipient of support, not the provider in the past claim.
rationales.The firm has been supported by local clu: The passive first clause reverses the past direction of support, making clubs support the firm.
rationales.The firm has supported local clubs and w: 'Has' needs 'supported', whereas 'continue to' needs 'support'. Giving each construction its required form preserves the firm as provider in both claims.
rationales.The firm has supported local clubs and h: The future relationship is reversed: this hopes for support from clubs instead of promising continuing support for them.

findings: Lesson-plan/seminar-discussion original repeated elementary designed-to matching and generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Coordinated auxiliaries with incompatible shared verb forms
audit.pedagogicalValue: Repeats a verb when two governing constructions cannot use one unchanged form.
audit.levelReason: Requires preserving tense and continuation meaning in a compressed editorial repair.
audit.similarityNote: Morphological sharing constraint, not simply choosing one participle after an auxiliary.

items.setupText: The proposal agrees with earlier recommendations, but its reasoning does not rely on them.
items.taskText: Which parallel description preserves both relationships?
options: The proposal is consistent with and dependent on earlier recommendations.
The proposal is consistent with, but does not depend on, earlier recommendations.
The proposal is neither consistent with nor dependent on earlier recommendations.
The proposal is dependent on, but not consistent with, earlier recommendations.
items.answer: The proposal is consistent with, but does not depend on, earlier recommendations.
items.explanation: The shared noun phrase completes two different predicates; the positive consistency claim and negative dependence claim remain intact.

rationales.The proposal is consistent with, but doe: The shared noun phrase completes two different predicates; the positive consistency claim and negative dependence claim remain intact.
rationales.The proposal is consistent with and depe: This makes the proposal dependent on the recommendations, contradicting the intended independence.
rationales.The proposal is neither consistent with: This wrongly denies consistency as well as dependence.
rationales.The proposal is dependent on, but not co: This reverses the two relationships, affirming reliance while denying agreement.

findings: Survey/risk-assessment original was one more repeated infinitive list without C1-level judgment.
audit.microSkill: Different predicate forms share a complement while preserving polarity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Balances related propositions without forcing identical voice, word class or polarity.
audit.levelReason: Requires maintaining two distinct conceptual relationships in compact coordination.
audit.similarityNote: One shared complement serves adjective and verbal predicates with different polarity.

items.setupText: An architect says: 'What matters is not whether the room is large but whether it can be adapted.'
items.taskText: How does the parallel whether-pair organize the assessment?
options: It establishes that the room is small but can be adapted.
It makes a large size necessary before adaptability can be considered.
It shifts the criterion from size to adaptability without settling either factual question.
It says that size and adaptability are equally necessary conditions.
items.answer: It shifts the criterion from size to adaptability without settling either factual question.
items.explanation: The balanced interrogative clauses contrast evaluation criteria rather than affirming or denying the room's properties.

rationales.It establishes that the room is small bu: The sentence changes what matters; it does not answer the embedded questions about this room.
rationales.It shifts the criterion from size to ada: The balanced interrogative clauses contrast evaluation criteria rather than affirming or denying the room's properties.
rationales.It makes a large size necessary before a: The first criterion is being set aside, not made a prerequisite for the second.
rationales.It says that size and adaptability are e: The corrective pair prioritizes adaptability instead of giving both criteria equal necessity.

findings: Manual/interviews-coded original supplied elementary list errors under advanced contextual wording.
audit.microSkill: Corrective parallel embedded questions distinguish criteria from facts
audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids reading a choice of assessment criterion as an answer to the questions themselves.
audit.levelReason: Requires separating evaluative focus from truth commitments inside a cleft-like construction.
audit.similarityNote: Interpretation of a whether-pair, unlike B2's explicit matching-clause style task.

items.setupText: The owner dismissed the chef; the chef then criticised the owner. Keep both actions as parallel noun phrases with the actor and target clear.
items.taskText: Which version preserves those roles?
options: The dispute involved the owner's dismissal of the chef and the chef's criticism of the owner.
The dispute involved the chef's dismissal of the owner and the owner's criticism of the chef.
The dispute involved the owner's dismissal and criticism of the chef.
The dispute involved the chef's dismissal and criticism of the owner.
items.answer: The dispute involved the owner's dismissal of the chef and the chef's criticism of the owner.
items.explanation: Each possessive names the actor, and each of-phrase names the target, preserving the reciprocal roles.

rationales.The dispute involved the chef's dismissa: This reverses who performed both actions.

The two clauses establish that each influence has exactly the same strength.
The direction of influence reverses as the two noun phrases exchange roles.

items.setupText: A meeting note says, 'Ava revised her proposal, and Mina did too.' Ava's proposal is her own; no context specifies the owner of the proposal Mina revised.

Either woman's proposal could be meant.
It shifts ownership to Mina when the subject changes.
It refers to a proposal jointly owned by the two women.
items.answer: Either woman's proposal could be meant.
items.explanation: The omitted wording can preserve Ava as the possessor or shift to the new subject, Mina. Without context, neither reading excludes the other.

The omitted wording can preserve Ava as the possessor or shift to the new subject, Mina. Without context, neither reading excludes the other.

findings: The report sentence repeated the C2 criticism list; its feedback treated optional preposition sharing as an error.

items.setupText: 'The museum and the theatre received grants of $40,000 and $60,000, respectively.' An editor wants to remove 'respectively' without changing the allocation.
items.taskText: Which revision makes the original pairings explicit?

The museum received $60,000, while the theatre received $40,000.
The museum and theatre shared a $40,000 grant and a $60,000 grant.
The museum received $40,000; the theatre received $60,000.

items.explanation: 'Respectively' pairs the first institution with the first amount and the second with the second; the revision states those two allocations.

rationales.The museum and theatre each received gra: 'Each' distributes both amounts to each institution rather than pairing one amount with each.
rationales.The museum received $60,000, while the t: This reverses the order-based pairing established by 'respectively'.
rationales.The museum received $40,000; the theatre: 'Respectively' pairs the first institution with the first amount and the second with the second; the revision states those two allocations.

findings: The schedule version offered the same criticism pattern with an evidentiary-hearing tail and generic feedback.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Expand respectively without turning separate allocations into joint or repeated awards.

audit.similarityNote: Tests ordered list-to-list mapping, not the headcount or both/either contrasts elsewhere.

items.setupText: 'Ruth promised the chair to withdraw the amendment and persuaded the secretary to record the decision.'
items.taskText: Which account correctly recovers the understood subjects of the two infinitives?
options: The chair would withdraw; the secretary would record.
Ruth would withdraw and record the decision.
Ruth would withdraw; the secretary would record.
The chair would withdraw; Ruth would record.
items.answer: Ruth would withdraw; the secretary would record.
items.explanation: With 'promise', the promiser undertakes the infinitive action; with 'persuade', the person persuaded is its understood subject. Similar surface patterns need not assign the same roles.

rationales.The chair would withdraw; the secretary: The chair receives the promise but is not the person promising to withdraw.
rationales.Ruth would withdraw and record the decis: Persuading the secretary assigns the intended recording action to the secretary, not Ruth.
rationales.The chair would withdraw; Ruth would rec: This reverses both relationships: Ruth undertakes the withdrawal, and the secretary is persuaded to record.
rationales.Ruth would withdraw; the secretary would: With 'promise', the promiser undertakes the infinitive action; with 'persuade', the person persuaded is its understood subject. Similar surface patterns need not assign the same roles.

findings: The form item used arbitration vocabulary without increasing the elementary list-form demand.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Recover agency from each governing verb rather than from a visually repeated noun-plus-infinitive pattern.
audit.levelReason: C2 requires resolving two different control relationships inside one coordinated sentence.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike C1 finite-versus-infinitive attachment, both target actions are infinitival but their governors assign different actors.

items.setupText: A researcher needs to identify a single amendment that the senate drafted and the council adopted. The question must not treat either event as already identified in a separate question.

options: Which amendment did the senate draft and the council adopt?
Which amendment did the senate draft, and what did the council adopt?
What did the senate draft, and which amendment did the council adopt?
Which amendment did the council adopt after the senate drafted its own?
items.answer: Which amendment did the senate draft and the council adopt?
items.explanation: The initial question phrase supplies the missing object of both 'draft' and 'adopt', so one amendment must satisfy both descriptions.

rationales.Which amendment did the senate draft, an: The separate 'what' question can seek a different object; it does not require the drafted and adopted amendment to be the same.
rationales.Which amendment did the senate draft and: The initial question phrase supplies the missing object of both 'draft' and 'adopt', so one amendment must satisfy both descriptions.
rationales.What did the senate draft, and which ame: This also asks two independently answerable object questions rather than identifying their shared object.

findings: The notice item repeated for-being/for-lacking/for-ignoring and supplied no explanation of permissible shared material.
audit.microSkill: One question phrase as the shared object of coordinated clauses
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguish a single shared-object question from two independent questions with similar wording.
audit.levelReason: C2 involves interpreting an extracted object across two different subjects and verbs.
audit.similarityNote: Unlike the sentence-boundaries shared-object split, this tests question reference rather than sentence punctuation.

items.setupText: A profile calls Inez 'a former chair and adviser to the foundation'. She has left both roles. The editor must state that without relying on how far 'former' extends.
items.taskText: Which wording unambiguously puts both coordinated roles in the past?

Inez previously chaired and advised the foundation.
Inez is an adviser and a former chair of the foundation.
Inez is a former chair who advises the foundation.
items.answer: Inez previously chaired and advised the foundation.
items.explanation: The shared past-time modifier applies to both past-tense verbs, explicitly describing the two roles as previous ones.

rationales.Inez previously chaired and advised the: The shared past-time modifier applies to both past-tense verbs, explicitly describing the two roles as previous ones.
rationales.Inez, formerly the chair, is an adviser: This puts only the chair role in the past and states a current adviser role.
rationales.Inez is an adviser and a former chair of: Moving the adviser role first still presents it as current; only 'chair' is marked former.
